KEY MESSAGE 1...
A mid-level shortwave on the northern end of a mid-level jet 
max is expected to cross into the area today, bringing with it 
chances of showers and thunderstorms. The 12Z would certainly 
not allude to severe chances with an 800mb and 600mb capping 
inversion, though there is some idea this profile will modulate 
into the afternoon with mid-level ascent, but the question is 
how much.

The most likely scenario is that capping doesn't erode fully, 
leaving a quasi-stable layer with fairly dry air above, which 
would suppress vertical development, and further any severe 
chances. In the low probability event that the caps fully 
erode, DCAPE valued from 800-1000 J/kg would be a double edged 
sword for development. This could serve to entrain dry air into 
updrafts with fairly weak forcing squashing development, or it 
could contribute to a downburst wind threat should updrafts 
develop vertically despite all odds. One way you might actualize
this is multiple failed CI attempts wet-bulbing profiles, or 
forcing stronger than forecast. All this to say, the severe 
environment is conditionally marginal, with a low probability 
of any damaging winds this afternoon in storms overall.

KEY MESSAGE 2...
As an eastern trough shifts east, and a Midwest ridge fills in
behind, the potential for upstream MCS development increases
into Monday and Tuesday, along with the chance of run-of-the-
mill afternoon convection. 

The chances of an actual MCS monday afternoon appear low for
now, but afternoon storm chances are certainly prevalent.
Diurnal heating and destabilization aloft pushed NBM 25th-75th
SBCAPE to 1000-2000 J/kg, and sfc-6km shear increases to 30kts
to 35kts, with the largest proportional increase to winds in 
the sfc-3km layer from the day prior. 25th to 75th HREF DCAPE 
shows 800 to 1000, certainly capable of downburst wind threats 
with high enough vertical development. That being said, there is
still a split in CAMs for convection presence/intensity Monday.
Models like the FV3/HRRR/ARW show more robust mid-level ascent 
and less capping with more widespread convection, while CAMs 
like the NAM/RGEM have weaker forcing and slightly more capping.
So, there is again a conditional probability for severe Monday,
perhaps more likely than Sunday. Downburst winds and torrential
downpours are most likely, though hail and isolated tornadoes 
could not be ruled out.

Overnight, uncertainties compound. The first will be the affect
of what happens Monday. If widespread severe occurs Monday, 
that would perhaps muddle the environment for overnight 
convection Monday night whether an MCS occurs or not. Second 
will be the exact position and timing of an MCS. While certainty
has increased in the last 24 hours, the windows are still fairly
wide for position and timing. At the moment, a best-guess 
envelope for an MCS passage is between 8pm Monday and 8am 
Tuesday, with a "best guess" location being anywhere between 
Indiana and eastern Ohio. In any event, a blow to eastern Ohio 
would have the highest chance of impacting our area. Should 
convection not occur Monday, the highest conditional threat 
severe window would be earlier in the night. This would bring 
the highest chance of damaging winds, with isolated tornadoes 
and a flash flooding threat. Should convection occur during the 
day Monday, the highest conditional threat of severe weather 
would be a later arrival perhaps, with slightly lower threats of
wind and tornadoes with diurnal cooling. Be sure to monitor the
forecast for updates as we draw closer.

Tuesday will again depend on what happens overnight Monday. If
an MCS occurs, severe threat would be conditionally lower and 
vise versa. Ensembles show some steepening lapse rates behind a 
cold front, but by then the mid-level jet has pushed east. 
Nonetheless, scattered storms remain possible with a marginal 
downburst threat, favoring south of I-70. NCAR ML, CSU ML, and 
CIPS agree with a more "mid-Atlantic" threat Tuesday.
